Abstract—The recent rapid spread of infectious diseases has
significantly strained healthcare systems globally, presenting risks
to both patients and frontline healthcare workers. In such
scenarios, critically ill individuals require hospitalization and
treatment by specialized intensive care teams. With the support
of increasingly intelligent, personalized, and assertive computing
technologies, health professionals can reach hospitalized patients
to make decisions, even when the disease involves a high risk of
contamination. This work presents a new remote cyber-physical
patient monitoring system using Computer Vision technologies
for decision-making support of the health team mainly working in
Intensive Care Units. The system can assist hospitalized patients
by continuously and contactlessly monitoring their vital functions
from the screen of any multiparametric monitor model, thus
being monitor-agnostic. Moreover, in support of such situations,
it can alert and detect critical problems before they deteriorate
and help provide comprehensive care with minimal doctor-patient
interaction.
Index Terms—remote patient monitoring, cyber-physical sys-
tem, computer vision, mobile alert application
I. INTRODUCTION
New forms of patient monitoring and care represent a
revolution in healthcare provided worldwide [1], [2]. With the
support of increasingly intelligent, personalized, and assertive
computing technologies such as cyber-physical systems [3],
doctors, nurses, and other health professionals can remotely
reach hospitalized patients and make decisions, even when
diseases involve a high risk of contamination like during
the COVID-19 pandemic [4]. This disease generated a catas-
trophic global health crisis, the most significant since the 1918
979-8-3503-8438-3/24/$31.00 2024 IEEE
influenza pandemic and resulted in over 3.8 million deaths
worldwide [5].
Critically ill people needed to be hospitalized in Intensive
Care Units (ICUs) and treated by critical care teams headed
up by intensivist doctors. This generates the need to treat
patients by providing constant and comprehensive care with
minimal doctor-patient interaction. Scientists worldwide affirm
that Coronavirus will not be the last pandemic in our lifetime.
In addition, they warn the threat posed by zoonoses (infectious
diseases that jump from animals to humans) is on the rise [6].
Therefore, we need to be better prepared to combat current
and emerging waves of pathogens, with our primary objective
in applications for health being to advance the field through
innovative technological solutions, enhancing healthcare de-
livery and outcomes.
Derived from artificial intelligence, Computer Vision has
played an essential role in digital transformation, among the
most promising technologies in the monitoring area. It uses
deep learning to catalog the images (static or dynamic) cap-
tured by cameras and sensors, supporting decision-making [7].
The approach using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
[8] is commonly applied in Computer Vision due to the
excellent results in image classification, object detection, and
recognition compared to other methods [9].
Methods used to improve the performance of CNNs further
follow a semantic segmentation approach of joint detection
of objects [10], [11], generally achieving good results. For
example, in the object detection task, the algorithm for Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) [12] converts images containing
text represented by characters into information that a machine


can understand. In addition, the latest Machine Learning
based systems can accommodate many different fonts and
image formats. However, this task presents varying recognition
difficulties, depending on the text’s structure, positioning, and
formatting. Traditional OCR methods define and apply various
filters to images to differentiate characters of interest from the
background, detect the contour to recognize individual charac-
ters, and use image classification algorithms to identify those
characters. When the text is standardized and clearly defined,
these protocols are usually sufficient, but this is not always the
case. Sometimes, it is impossible to separate the characters in
the detection phase, either due to the diversified positioning
of the text or the low resolution of the images, lighting
problems, or even noise that makes it difficult to distinguish
them accurately. In these cases, specialized approaches based
on Deep Learning have been applied, producing promising
results [13]. Some Deep Learning algorithms can currently
identify the input image and assign various essential char-
acteristics through CNNs, involving processing, analysis, and
identification activities as complex as human vision.
One of the most popular libraries for Computer Vision,
OpenCV [14], offers integration with Tesseract open source
OCR engine [12], [15], a module currently capable of apply-
ing Deep Learning as a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
network, generating a robust OCR tool. Within the OpenCV
framework, it is possible to first use a text detector like EAST
[12], an efficient and accurate scene text detector, to identify
the position of the text and then interpret it using Tesseract.
In addition to Tesseract, other modern OCR applications can
achieve satisfactory results in extracting text from images, such
as ABBYY FineReader, Google Cloud Vision API, Microsoft
Vision API ReadIris, Paddle OCR, and OmniPage, among
others. In addition to all these possibilities, there are also
APIs from the leading providers of Cloud Computing services.
For example, Google, Amazon, and Microsoft provide specific
platforms for recognizing text in images. AWS Amazon Tex-
tract [16], for instance, is a service that combines proprietary
OCR technologies with Machine Learning to automatically
extract text (printed or handwritten) and data from scanned
documents.
In short, several technologies exist to recognize characters
and words in images, store them and convert them into
textual formats, and facilitate data analysis and manipulation.
Some are robust against noise, distortions, style variations,
translations, and rotations. However, this comes with a price
in terms of services, justifying searching for low-cost and ef-
fective alternative solutions. A detailed compilation of modern
solutions using OCR is available in [17].
This work presents SENTINELA, a new remote cyber-
physical patient monitoring system using Computer Vision
technologies for decision-making support of the health team
mainly working in Intensive Care Units (ICUs). These are
vital departments of a hospital to enhance the survival of
critically ill patients. The system was developed to assist
hospitalized patients by enabling continuous and contactless
monitoring of their vital functions from the screen of any
multiparametric monitor model, thus being monitor-agnostic.
Moreover, it can alert and detect critical problems before
they deteriorate and help to provide comprehensive care with
minimal doctor-patient interaction. Importantly, our project has
received ethical approval from the Research Ethics Committee,
enabling comprehensive clinical studies in Instituto Dr. Jos´e
Frota’s ICU, a tertiary-level hospital within Brazil’s Unified
Health System.
II. SYSTEM OVERVIEW
A. System Architecture
The system’s architecture of SENTINELA, shown in Figure
1, is an event-driven architecture (EDA), which is a type
of service-oriented architecture (SOA) [18], [19]. It also in-
cludes: (1) A physical device we named EVA (Equipment for
Visualization and Alerts) [20] to help monitor the patient’s
health through Computer Vision coupled with the screen of
the hospital’s ICU multiparametric monitor, (2) the EVA AWS
server, and (3) the frontend mobile alert application named
EDEN.
The multiparametric monitor is a medical device for con-
tinuously monitoring the patient’s health status, such as heart
rate, blood pressure (systolic, diastolic, and mean), blood oxy-
gen saturation, respiratory rate, and human body temperature
through sensors attached to the patient’s body. The mean blood
pressure can be calculated from the systolic and diastolic
pressures [21].
In Figure 1, the components external to the darker grey rect-
angle with dotted lines are native AWS services, while those
within the outlined area are containerized services developed
by the SENTINELA team.
Fig. 1: SENTINELA architecture.
Diving deeper into the AWS services we used, the following
details are provided:
SQS Managed message queue service that allows asyn-
chronous event-oriented communication between SEN-
TINELA’s services.
RDS Managed relational database service where the patient,
bed, and health care team data are stored.


AMP Managed service for Prometheus [22], a monitoring
and alerting tool that includes a time series database.
The service is used to store the vital functions monitor
readings over time and manage critical values alerts.
S3 Managed service for object storage used by SENTINELA’s
project team to store the vital signs captured by the EVAs
devices from the multiparametric monitors that are later
recognized by the OCR service.
All AWS services utilized are deployed and managed in
the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) model with Terraform [23],
an automation and deployment management tool for cloud
applications, to maximize the reproducibility of environments
and increase productivity by reusing common infrastructure
components in the production of deployment variations. In
addition, it allows for perfect replicas of the production envi-
ronment to be created for testing and development purposes.
The services implemented in the context of the SEN-
TINELA system include:
SENTINELA-backend Service which facilitates communica-
tion for each EVA device when it connects to the
internet to update its settings and periodically transmit
images of the patient’s bed vital signs multiparametric
monitor. This service also generates an event in the
architecture that will trigger the OCR service to recognize
the health indicators monitored.
SENTINELA-ocr Service that uses computer vision and ar-
tificial intelligence techniques to recognize the indicators
in the image with the readings from the vital functions
of the multiparametric monitor, generating a success or
failure event in the reading that will later be processed
by the SENTINELA-crud.
SENTINELA-crud Service responsible for mediating access
to the system’s databases and responding to queries made
by the applications accessible by the medical team. This
is the only service in the structure with access to all neces-
sary patient data, beds, health team, and multiparametric
monitor readings history.
In our system, all services are deployed as Kubernetes
Deployments. For the crud and backend services, these De-
ployments will be horizontally scaled based on a percentile
of the latency of their HTTP request processing, using the
HPA [24] that will monitor these metrics which are stored in
Prometheus. On the other hand, the OCR service will have
its horizontal scalability managed with the help of KEDA
[25]. KEDA will be configured to increase or decrease the
number of replicas of the service based on the number of EVAs
transmitting images to the system. All the container running
infrastructure is executed on AWS Fargate, an AWS native
serverless container service, in the EKS cluster. AWS Fargate
is a serverless capacity provider from AWS, where containers
are run on Kubernetes nodes [26] managed by AWS, and the
AWS service itself determines how many and which nodes
to allocate based on the resources requested by each running
Pod. In short, the workflow shown in Figure 1 is as follows:
1. An admin user registers a new EVA device in the system
through the admin app, communicating with the SEN-
TINELA’s service.
2. The SENTINELA-crud publishes an event that triggers
the creation of a new OCR instance.
3. Each EVA device publishes an image to the backend
service.
4. The backend service saves the image to the S3.
5. The backend service publishes a new image available
event.
6. The OCR service receives the event and starts processing
the image and the crud service registers the arrival of the
image.
7. The OCR fetches the image from the S3 and processes
it.
8. The OCR publishes a new image processed event or a
failure to process event.
9. The CRUD service consumes the event.
10. The CRUD service stores the image’s metadata on the
PostgreSQL (RDS) database and the health indicators on
the Prometheus database.
11. The health team app is used to query the health indicators
of a patient.
B. Physical and Electronic Structures of the EVA Device
We started designing an original 3D digital model of the
EVA device (shown on the left side of Figure 1), including
its internal structures. Then, we used 3D printing technology
to create it as a 3D real-world object, as shown in Figure 2.
Its physical structure consists of four main parts (Figure 3): a
bracket for coupling to a multiparametric monitor, a “neck”,”
a camera case, and a power supply.
Item 1 of Figure 3 shows EVA’s bracket. It can be fixed on
the top of any multiparametric monitor model with adhesive,
clamp, glue, or screw. It may have one or more support points
to provide greater stability to the equipment. In addition, the
bracket may need (or not) an inclination adjustment to avoid
hiding the data visualization displayed on the screen of the
multiparametric monitor.
From a linear movement, attached to the fixed bracket is
the EVA’s neck (item 2 of Figure 3). This structure allows
the positional adjustment of EVA’s camera relative to the
multiparametric monitor, allowing its use in devices with
varied screen sizes. We created a displacement system for this
mobile EVA structure that works by sliding its neck and a
part of the fixed bracket. In addition, we designed sockets in
EVA’s neck to lock the desired position of the camera. The
camera case (item 3 of Figure 3) houses all the electronics
built-in EVA, connecting to the rest of the structure from
an articulation point at the end of the EVA’s neck. This
articulation point enables a correction of the monitor screen
viewing angle if adjustments are made to the distance from
the monitor, making possible varied angles for positioning the
EVA’s camera, which facilitates finding an optimum image
quality to be captured.
We have also developed the EVA’s electronic structure
model, which corresponds to a minimal device capable of cap-


Fig. 2: An EVA device in operation, coupled to a hospital’s
ICU physiological multiparametric monitor.
Fig. 3: The 3D digital model of the EVA’s physical structure
coupled to the physiological multiparametric monitor: (1) fixed
bracket, (2) “neck”, (3) camera case, and (4) power supply.
turing an image displayed on the screen of a multiparametric
monitor and sending it to a cloud server. It consists of an
ESP32-CAM module, with an integrated camera and a high-
performance processor with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connection.
We designed EVA to embed a PCI card to accommodate
the ESP32-CAM module and add peripherals to visualize
events, facilitate connection to the power supply, and adjust
the module to its physical structure. Its electronic scheme is
formed by: a voltage regulator circuit and resistors to control
the input voltage of the camera’s power supply, a D2 diode
to protect the device, capacitors that work as filters preventing
voltage drops during data transmission, and resistors and flags
of the communication status with the cloud server. Finally,
we developed EVA’s firmware using the Arduino IDE and C
language.
The EVA device operates in a user-friendly and straightfor-
ward manner. To avoid saturating the image database and to
focus on evaluating the OCR’s performance, we have config-
ured the system to capture images at longer intervals, ranging
from one minute to one day, rather than every 3 seconds,
for instance. At each pre-set interval, the camera module
captures an image from the screen of the multiparametric
monitor, connects to the Internet via a router, uploads the
image to the web server (Figure 1), and then deactivates the
camera and Wi-Fi module to conserve energy and prevent
component overheating. The device continues this cycle indef-
initely, unless technical issues arise. Additionally, the image
quality can be adjusted remotely to various resolutions by the
server. Moreover, we have also designed and implemented
a lean Android application to facilitate the configuration of
system parameters on the EVA device, for example, those
related to the network, data access, and intensive care unit bed
identification which relates to a specific hospitalized patient.
This application connects with EVA, which, in turn, signals
with its LEDs that the connection was successful and data
were received and sent successfully.
C. OCR Implementation in the System
Vital signs are the standard indicators to assess a patient’s
health status. Human body temperature (in °C), heart rate
(in BPM), blood oxygen saturation (in %), respiratory rate
(breaths/min), and blood pressure with systolic and diastolic
(in mmHg) are the most common vital signs that help de-
termine a patient’s health [21]. At the center of vital signs
monitoring some sensors continue to enable the ability to
monitor and track conditions.
We devised a novel computer vision methodology to extract
patient vital data from multiparametric monitor screens, com-
prising three distinct steps. First, for each predefined display
layout of vital functions available in the system’s settings,
we define the Points Of Interest (POIs) on this layout, and
enclose them by their respective bounding areas, totaling seven
in all. Once set, these POIs are applied to all subsequent
captured images. If the display layout changes, the POIs need
only be redefined once on a base image. Examples of POI
annotations are shown in (a) of Figure 4. In the second step,
the areas determined by the previously specified bounding
boxes are cropped and passed through an OCR module. More
specifically, for this work, we used two different algorithms:
Paddle OCR [27] and Tesseract OCR [28]. Finally, we use
a straightforward whitelist filtering approach to selectively
remove irrelevant results from any noisy image patches.
Additionally, we developed another similar process, in-
cluding a preprocessing step using a perspective correction
algorithm to address distortion from the EVA device’s image
capture angle. To implement this, we used the OpenCV
library [29]. To apply the algorithm, we defined the region of
the image containing only the screen of the multiparametric
monitor, resulting in an Oriented Bounding Box (OBB). Then
the POIs in the perspective-corrected image were redefined to
correspond to their locations in the distorted image.
The implementation of POIs significantly reduces the com-
plexity of the task of detecting and recognizing measurements,
eliminating the need for more sophisticated techniques such as
Named Entity Recognition [30] or Document Understanding
[31]. However, it makes the system more vulnerable to small
misalignments that may occur in the image capture device,
either due to vibrations or changes in the layout of the
screen selected by the healthcare professional on-site. To
address this issue, it is possible to provide multiple layout
adjustments by configuring predefined sets of bounding boxes
for each possible screen configuration. Another approach is to
implement a customization tool where the user can define the
regions of the screen corresponding to each POI.
During monitoring, critical situations may occur. For ex-
ample, sometimes the patient’s blood pressure is so low that

(d) An example of alert (yellow area). Image captured at night.

it can not be measured. When this happens, in the place of
numerical values, “XX/XX” and “xx” appear on the screen of
the multiparametric monitor, as shown in (c) of Figure 4. Also,
health monitoring relies on the small wearable sensors attached
to the patient’s body (for example, stuck to the skin, clipped
on the fingers, etc.), carrying vital signs information to the
multiparametric monitor. Therefore, another challenging prob-
lem occurs when a voluntary or involuntary user movement
causes motion artifacts or even when a sensor is not working
the way it should, altering the overall quality of the signals
obtained and displayed on the screen of the multiparametric
monitor. Hence, these problems may corrupt the resulting
measurements, as shown in the upper middle in (c) and bottom
right in (d) of Figure 4, respectively, having “- -” and “- -/- -”
as a result for the blood oxygen saturation and pressure values.
Finally, during monitor alerts, the colour tones of specific POIs
sometimes alter, as shown in the yellow region at the top left
of the screen in (d) of Figure 4, creating difficulties for the
image filters, consequently making it difficult to recognize the
characters.
D. Mobile Alert Application: EDEN
To address the need for enhanced monitoring of hospitalized
patients by medical teams, we opted for a monitoring solution
involving firmware and database infrastructure, paired with a
user-interface mobile application. In the EDEN mobile appli-
cation (shown on the left side of Figure 1), the user interface
was developed in JavaScript using React Native library [32],
enabling execution on both iOS and Android mobile devices. It
features vital sign indicators for each monitored patient. These
indicators include human body temperature (Temp), heart rate
(HR), blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), respiratory rate (RR),
and blood pressure (BP) with systolic (SBP) and diastolic
(DBP) values. React Native facilitated the implementation of
functionalities to add ICUs, hospital beds in an ICU, and
patients to a bed, enabling health teams to virtually manage
monitored areas.
Additionally, a user registration feature was implemented,
requiring credentials and user profiles (doctor, physiotherapist,
nurse, etc.) to ensure data access is limited to authorized users.
Particularly, the functionality to add new patients is available
to authorized health team members and can be viewed by
others, respecting the team’s hierarchy and roles.
For patient monitoring, the app includes a module for
data retrieval and consolidation, graphically displaying each
patient’s vital signs over time. We used Prometheus [33],
configured to fetch vital signs data from a database at pre-set
intervals (currently every 5 seconds). Grafana [34] was em-
ployed for graph customization, including chart type (linear),
refresh rate (5 seconds), alarm thresholds (based on medical
guidelines) [21], and visualization attributes (color, font, title,
layout, highlights, etc.). Finally, the application integrates an
alarm system with Prometheus through AlertManager [35],
configured to send Telegram messages to registered and au-
thorized users when patients’ vital signs deviate from normal
ranges for a predetermined period (currently set at 10 seconds).
Figure 5 shows the main screens of the EDEN mobile appli-
cation. We chose Telegram for its ease of integration and cost-
effectiveness in our prototype. AlertManager supports multiple
notification methods, including SMS, Slack, e-mail, and voice
calls. Future versions of our system will explore these options
to enhance accessibility and meet diverse user needs.
In this example, for the patient in bed 1, referring to the
values collected at 22:10 as displayed on the main screens of
the EDEN mobile app, the following observations are made:
HR (Heart Rate) at 124 BPM is elevated, surpassing the
normal adult range of 60 to 100 BPM. SpO2 (Oxygen Sat-
uration) is at the upper normal limit of 100%, with the typical
range being 95% to 100%. SBP (Systolic Blood Pressure)
and DBP (Diastolic Blood Pressure) are 196 mmHg and 144
mmHg, respectively, both exceeding the normal ranges of 90
to 120 mmHg for SBP and 60 to 80 mmHg for DBP. TEMP


Fig. 5: Some of the main screens of the EDEN mobile application.
(Temperature) is at a normal 37°C, aligning with the average
of 37°C (98.6°F). RR (Respiratory Rate) stands at an elevated
31 RPM, above the normal adult rate of 12 to 16 breaths
per minute. Thus, the most concerning values here are the
elevated heart rate (HR) of 124 BPM, the high systolic (SBP)
and diastolic blood pressures (DBP) of 196 mmHg and 144
mmHg respectively, and the elevated respiratory rate (RR) of
31 RPM. These values, particularly the blood pressure and
heart rate, should be clinically evaluated by the health team.
III. EARLY EVALUATIONS OF THE SYSTEM’S
COMPONENTS
In this section, we present early evaluations of the EVA
device, examining its physical and electronic structures and
the performance of the OCR component. These evaluations
are important for assessing the device’s practicality, efficiency,
and adaptability in a healthcare setting before conducting end-
to-end system tests—from image capture to OCR processing
and mobile application integration. They also help determine
the OCR module’s effectiveness in accurately processing and
analyzing images.
In the evaluation process, the involvement of two senior
members in cloud computing and visual computing played
a fundamental role. Their responsibilities included scrutiniz-
ing relevant aspects, providing strategic guidance, suggesting
enhancements, and guiding the development team through
the development process. Additionally, the collaboration of
a medical expert in ICU care played a key role in defining
the system requirements, leading to ongoing improvements
and refinements in both the EVA device and the mobile
alert application. This not only addressed hospital needs and
informed the parameters for OCR tests of parametric vital sign
monitors but also smoothly integrated into the project devel-
opment. Consequently, this collaboration resulted in valuable
suggestions for enhancements at various stages of research,
thereby driving an iterative and productive cycle of learning,
development, and testing.
A. Evaluation of EVA Device: Physical and Electronic Struc-
tures
In our extensive evaluation and stress testing, the EVA
device underwent rigorous hours of continuous monitoring to
verify consistent functionality under stress, particularly with
high image loads. We tested its ability to capture images in
various resolutions, day and night, optimizing performance for
the OCR module. Additionally, we developed and tested four
versions of the EVA design, each iteration improving design
features, usability, and adaptability to different multiparametric
monitor models. These tests were fundamental in refining the
EVA’s physical structure.
Even as prototypes, the EVA device components proved
useful, flexible, and versatile in hospital ICU settings. The
bracket attaches securely to various multiparametric monitor
models, offering stability and adjustable inclination to prevent
screen obstruction. The “neck” allows for adaptable camera
positioning across different monitor sizes, and the camera
case facilitates angle adjustments for optimal image capture.
Built around an ESP32-CAM module, the electronic struc-
ture underwent rigorous testing to validate its efficiency in
capturing and transmitting images to a cloud server, ensuring
the device’s reliability and effectiveness in real-world hospital
environments.
B. Performance Evaluation of the System’s OCR
The evaluation of our solution was conducted on a sample
of 523 images featuring critical health situations. Accuracy
was evaluated overall and for each vital sign metric, including
blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), human body temperature
(Temp), respiratory rate (RR), heart rate (HR), and blood
pressure (the mean BP, with systolic (SBP) and diastolic
(DBP)), considering a hit when the entire field string was
correctly identified.
The analysis included two scenarios: (1) Evaluating the
entire validation set (second and fourth columns of Tables I
and II), and (2) Focusing on a subset of screens with non-
empty, extractable values, thus, excluding images with empty
fields in the measurements (“- -” and the “- -/- -” characters
from the sample), shown in the third and fifth columns of
Tables I and II.
Regarding the OCR module’s functionality, two distinct
algorithms were assessed: Paddle OCR [27] and Tesseract
OCR [28]. The complete comparative analysis of the results
is shown in Tables I and II.

These results demonstrate the better performance of the
Paddle OCR solution over the Tesseract OCR algorithm in
all test scenarios. Among the tests conducted with Tesseract,
the result for the heart rate metric stands out as it signifi-
cantly underperformed compared to the other metrics in its
original perspective. However, this was greatly improved when
perspective correction was applied. The perspective correction
did not provide significant advantages for the other metrics.
Qualitative analysis of the results revealed that the Tesser-
act algorithm did not perform well in situations involving
alarm signage, where the background and foreground colors
alternated between yellow and black, as well as in situations
involving decimal points, as shown in Figure 6.
In contrast, the tests with the Paddle OCR algorithm yielded
near-perfect results with minimal variations across the metrics.
The perspective correction did not have a significant impact
on the overall performance of the solution. Among the errors
encountered in recognition with this algorithm, only errors due
to noise in the smaller bounding box of the corresponding
mean pressure measurement were observed. This error arises
from the need to expand the bounding box to encompass
situations where the measurements consist of 2 or 3 characters,
as shown in Figure 7. Such errors can be corrected by
improving post-processing techniques, such as applying regex
(regular expression) techniques [36].
In the current version of our system, Paddle OCR errors may
lead to false alarms or missed alarms. While false alarms may
inconvenience medical professionals without directly risking
patient safety, missed alarms can overlook critical patient
needs. To mitigate this, we reduce the interval between image
captures to increase the likelihood of detecting missed readings
in subsequent frames. Ongoing clinical validation studies are
also continuously enhancing OCR accuracy and reliability.

To conclude, the best results were achieved with the Paddle
OCR algorithm without image preprocessing, i.e., without
applying warping, so it was selected for integration into the
current version of our SENTINELA system pipeline.
IV. CONCLUDING REMARKS AND FUTURE WORK
ICUs generate vast quantities of image data depicting pa-
tients in critical conditions. In this work, we introduced a
novel remote cyber-physical patient monitoring system de-
signed for ICUs. This system continuously and contactlessly
monitors patients’ vital functions from any multiparametric
monitor screen, alerting about critical health issues before they
deteriorate and aiding the decision-making process. It allows
patient care without requiring specialists like cardiologists and
nephrologists to be constantly at the bedside, thus reducing
the health team’s workload, especially during high-demand
periods such as the pandemic. Additionally, it minimizes
biosafety risks by reducing the need for physical contact.
In our comprehensive evaluation and stress testing, the EVA
device consistently demonstrated reliability under high image
load conditions and varying lighting, essential for effective
OCR performance. The iterative design process made the de-
vice adaptable to different multiparametric monitor models and
ICU operational needs. The final prototypes were functional
and versatile, efficiently capturing and transmitting images for
cloud-based analysis. Using the Paddle OCR algorithm, our
solution achieved near-perfect accuracy with minimal variation
across metrics, and perspective correction had a negligible


impact on performance. Some findings suggest areas for
refinement, notably noise in small bounding boxes for mean
pressure measurements, especially when accommodating two
or three characters.
Building on insights from preliminary testing, our future
work will involve conducting detailed performance analytics
of the microservices architecture in a simulated environment,
followed by field tests in a hospital ICU setting in collabo-
ration with our healthcare team partners. This approach will
encompass user interaction and the developed backend storage,
ensuring a comprehensive evaluation. Additionally, we plan
to examine user opinions, particularly those of clinicians and
other health teams, regarding SENTINELA’s usefulness and
actual effectiveness in such sensitive environments (ICUs).
Finally, it is worth mentioning that the system we have been
developing does not aim to replace the health team but, instead,
to add value by using new technologies for monitoring. These
can help hospitals and medical facilities respond to patient
emergencies remotely, securely, and contactless as soon as a
problem arises.
